summary: Slot eviction cascade triggered by ephemeral logging flood in customer's dedicated pool causing sustained p99 throughput regression
description:
Issue summary:
During midday traffic on 2026-03-09 Tellara Health observed a sustained p99 throughput regression and increased error tail for batched text-generation routes on their dedicated pool. Customers reported timeouts and elevated latency for short-stream and batched routes. Impact was observed across their pinned model variants.

Impact:
- Customer-facing throughput p99 increased from ~220ms to >2.1s for batched routes for ~45 minutes.
- Several requests timed out and triggered client-side retries, increasing downstream load.
- Autoscaler triggered multiple partial shrink/grow cycles and several slot evictions.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool id: dp-tellara-02
- Region: us-east
- Models pinned: gpt-open-8b v1, redwood-1.2 v3
- Serving runtime: 2026.02.11-canary build

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1. During the incident window a customer-side background job emitted a burst of ephemeral debug logs over stdout from many short-lived connections (third-party telemetry sidecar).
2. Sidecar log streams created transient high write QPS to disk-attached NVMe volumes on hosts hosting the dedicated pool.
3. Increased host IO latency delayed sidecar container heartbeats and health-check updates to the allocator.
4. Allocator interpreted delayed heartbeat + increased attach latency as slot slowness and started eviction cascades (attempting to rebalance).
5. Evictions caused transient loss of prefetch/kv-cache warm state and extra attach work — per-request latency increased, which fed back into autoscaler decisions and additional slot churn.
6. The cycle sustained for ~45m until mitigation applied.

Observed diagnostics and logs:
- NVMe write latency spikes correlated with the incident window on 6 hosts (host-az1-0[12-17]).
- Allocator logs: repeated lease-evict attempts and attach timeouts at p95/p99.
- Autoscaler logs: multiple shrink decisions at 1m granularity (+ immediate partial re-adds).
- Serving runtime: increased prefetched-kv-miss rate (cache miss ratio up from 3% to 48%).
- Monitoring: network IO for sidecars spiked, disk stall rate increased, GPU utilization showed short drops during attach/evict windows.

Notes about customer-side factors:
- Tellara's sidecar was introduced as a lightweight telemetry agent to stream logs; it had default batch size and a debug mode that was accidentally enabled in a recent deploy. This increased write amplification.
- The customer's workload included many short-lived model calls (chatlets) which are sensitive to warm KV cache and attach latency.

Business/Customer impact statement:
Tellara reported production user-facing slowdowns and a spike in their error budget during the window. Their incident response escalated to CS and requested a post-incident summary and follow-ups for avoidance of recurrence.

investigation_notes: Correlation analysis shows sidecar disk write bursts preceded allocator attach timeouts by ~18-30s.
Hosts with highest disk stalls had colocated GPUs serving the Tellara pool; those hosts experienced short-term GPU utilization drops as attach work increased.
Autoscaler responded to increased latency by shrinking (threshold triggers) which then created additional cold-attach work when traffic resumed, amplifying throughput regression.
No evidence of model-level correctness regressions; root cause is infrastructure IO pressure from ephemeral logging writes causing allocator heartbeat jitter.
Capacity floor was reached on several nodes due to prefetch eviction; observed p99 across client routes correlated with kv-cache cold misses.
root_cause: Transient host-level NVMe write amplification generated by a customer telemetry sidecar in debug mode. The resulting IO stalls delayed allocator heartbeats and attach operations, which the allocator interpreted as slow slots and triggered evictions. Evictions caused KV-cache loss and attach overhead, driving an autoscaler oscillation and sustained p99 throughput regression.
resolution:
Short-term: isolated affected hosts via host-drain and increased autoscaler cooldown to prevent immediate re-oscillation. Coordinated with the customer to rollback the telemetry sidecar debug flag which stopped the NVMe write storm.
Medium-term: merged allocator PR to increase heartbeat jitter tolerance and added a host IO stall detector to avoid eviction cascades triggered by non-GPU slowness.
Customer communicated that their deploy was reverted and service metrics returned to baseline within ~30 minutes of mitigation.
rollback_and_mitigation:
- Host-level isolation (drain) prevented new attaches to noisy nodes.
- Autoscaler cooldown increased from 1m to 5m for the pool to avoid churn while we stabilized.
- Customer reverted sidecar debug mode.
- Provided customer with recommendations to avoid high-frequency ephemeral disk writes (batching, rate-limits, disable debug).
next_steps: (Platform) Monitor dp-tellara-02 for 72h after incident; run autoscaler sims to validate cooldown changes do not reduce capacity responsiveness.
(Eng) Roll out allocator heartbeat tolerance patch to staging and two small production regions; track eviction rate metric delta. PR #1428.
(CS) Provide Tellara with post-incident guidance doc and a recommended sidecar config template for dedicated pools.
(SRE) Implement host IO stall alert and link it into runbook to avoid misclassifying host IO issues as slot performance problems.
(Security/Platform) Evaluate whether sidecar can be sandboxed to limit guest IO amplification on dedicated hosts; propose runtime cgroup/io throttling policy.
